It was three fifteen in the morning, and the laboratory was silent except for the hum of the coolers. Sahar Nouri sat curled up in her chair, looking at the screen, where the model was drawing something out of shapeless gray for the thousandth time.

She always thought of it as “static,” not “noise.” Her father had been a television repairman for twenty-eight years. In his little shop, among burned-out tubes and tangled wires, whenever the antenna failed and the screen filled with trembling specks, he would say, “This is everything that could have been shown.” In those days Sahar thought he was joking.

Now she knew he had not been joking. The static at step one thousand contained every image: every face, every room, every sea, and none of them. The model was not making anything. Step by step, it reduced the fog, and each time, from among what remained possible, it kept what was most compatible with the previous step. It was not creation. It was refinement. It was selection.

Near step four hundred, something happened that Sahar had been staring at for months. The image was still little more than a stain, but suddenly two paths opened before it. If it went left, a window appeared; if right, a wall. And what was frightening and beautiful was that choosing one path did not make the other “forbidden”; it merely made it distant. From the left-hand path, there was no way to reach something that belonged to the right-hand path—not because a law prevented it, but because the threads leading there had never met.

In her notebook she called these points “nodes.” Nodes that were possible only in certain regions of the world, because the route to them passed through only certain neighborhoods. The world could not become just anything; the world could become whatever was reachable from the heart of its yesterday.

Her tea had gone cold. Sahar reviewed it: the model does not begin from nothing. It begins from everything.

Step nine hundred ninety-nine. The gray stain took on color. Step one thousand. The image stopped.

It was a small room with a soldering table, tins of screws, and lamps Sahar had known since childhood. She could almost smell the tin and rosin. A television sat switched off on the table, and opposite it a full-length mirror leaned against the wall. The mirror reflected the television. And in the television’s dark glass, faintly, a woman could be seen curled up in a chair, looking at the screen.

Sahar held her breath. No such scene existed anywhere in the training data. She knew because she had built the data herself.

She opened the log. The prompt field was empty. In the row labeled “conditioning source,” there was only one word: unknown.

Her hands went cold. She had not written a prompt. So either someone had written one, or no one had needed to.

Sahar did not sleep until morning. Her first act was to repeat the exact same run, with the same settings and the same seed: zero. The image emerged from the static again, with the same branching at step four hundred, and again the same room, the same mirror, the same woman curled up in the chair. Byte for byte identical.

It was both the most reassuring thing imaginable and the most frightening. The noise she called “random” was not random; it was a function of a number. With seed one, an empty plain appeared; with seed seven, a smiling face. She tested a thousand seeds and none produced the room. The room appeared only with zero.

At seven she called Arman. Arman taught philosophy of physics and arrived with two cups of coffee and disheveled hair. He stared silently at the screen for a while.

“So your static isn’t random.”

“Pseudorandom. One number, one path.”

“Then Laplace was right. A demon that knew the position and velocity of every particle would see the future as it sees the past.”

“But I don’t know what will come out before each run. I have to run it.”

Arman smiled. “Exactly. Wolfram calls it computational irreducibility: some processes have no shortcut. The only way to know the result is to go through the path itself. There is determinism, but not prediction.”

“So the Laplacean demon would have to run the universe itself?”

“And a demon that runs the universe is no longer an observer. It is the universe. Perhaps that is why no one can stand above its path and say, ‘It was known in advance,’ because that ‘in advance’ is created only by the going.”

Sahar stared at zero. “So is the seed the same as ‘Be’?”

“No. The seed does not say what should happen; it only says where to begin. The rest is determined by the neighborhoods. What you call a prompt is the command that bends the path toward something. And you say that this time there was no command.”

“Just one word: unknown.”

Arman put down his coffee. “Then see whether this happens without your model and without your machine. If the room truly comes from the zero seed, it should appear on any machine.”

Sahar loaded the weights onto another server in the building, entered seed zero, and waited. The fog split step by step. At step four hundred the branch appeared; it followed the same path. The room, the soldering table, the mirror—all the same.

Except for one thing. This time the television on the table was on. And on its screen there was neither a face nor a room. Only static.

Before shutting down the model, Sahar took a photograph of the screen and sent it to Arman. Two minutes later the reply came: “Did you know that about one percent of the static on old televisions is cosmic background radiation? An echo of the Big Bang.”

She read it again and again. Her father had watched that static for years without knowing that, within it, there was also a remnant of the beginning of the universe.

At noon she sat facing Arman’s board. Arman wrote: “The information of a message is how impossible it is for you to guess it. Shannon measured this. Static is completely unpredictable, so it has maximum information.”

“And minimum meaning.”

“Exactly. Meaning is selection: keeping one message from among all possible messages and setting the rest aside. That is compression.”

“My model does exactly that.”

“And so do you when you speak. Every sentence you say discards millions of sentences left unsaid. The universe is full of information; selection makes meaning.”

Sahar said quietly, “Then the room had meaning. Someone, something, had kept it from the static.”

“That is the question. Who? Or what?”

At dusk, she turned in the key her mother had kept in a kitchen drawer for three years and unlocked the shop. Dust and solder. Rows of televisions that had never been repaired. There was no mirror and no table that could be matched to the model’s image. Only the same soldering table, the same lamps. The model’s room was her father’s shop, with something in it that had not been there.

In the drawer beneath the table she found a notebook. Its pages were filled with diagrams: lines that forked, nodes that never met, and at the end of one branch a rectangle like a television screen. Beneath it was one word: unknown.

Sahar could hardly breathe. The last page was dated two weeks before her father’s death and contained one sentence in the same crooked, familiar handwriting:

“If the static ever answers, do not touch zero.”

In the morning Arman found six public models from six different laboratories, and Sahar entered seed zero into all six. Six images appeared: a beach, an old man’s face, a rainy street, two abstract landscapes, and a cat. None was the room; none had the soldering table, mirror, and television.

“So zero isn’t magic. Zero is simply here in your model.”

Sahar stared at the table for a while. Then, as if confessing something, she said, “Last year, after Dad died, I scanned all his notebooks and repair manuals. Three thousand pages, about a thousand photographs of the shop. I trained a small personal layer on them. I never told anyone.”

Arman nodded slowly. “Then half the mystery is solved. The room is a node that exists only in the neighborhood of your model, because only here have three paths met: your father’s shop-world, the structure of diffusion, and the zero seed. In the other six models those paths never converged. That is what a neighboring possibility is. Every world can show only what is reachable from its yesterday.”

“But the mirror facing the television was in none of those photographs. I checked.”

“Exactly. That is where recombination begins. You had the materials, not their arrangement. Half of this can be explained, and half still cannot.”

Arman turned the pages of her father’s notebook, sometimes looking up. Near the end he found a page whose margins were filled with hand-drawn formulas, and in the middle, in a trembling hand, several sentences:

“A receiver makes nothing. It merely becomes resonant with one of the waves. The air is full of waves; all stations are always here. What you call seeing is only your tuning.”

Arman read it and raised his head slowly. “Your father reached something that we explain with PhDs and stacks of papers. A radio receiver selects one frequency from countless frequencies not by creating it, but by resonating with it. Resonance. And a receiver becomes resonant only where its structure matches the wave: a receiver receives according to its capacity.”

“Ibn Arabi said something like this too.”

“And Wheeler, the physicist who said the universe is built from yes-or-no questions. Every selection is a bit. ‘It from bit.’ If he was right, the observer does not add something from outside the universe. The observer is a way the universe selects.”

Sahar said softly, “Then the receiver is also the prompt. Its tuning says which wave.”

“And who did the tuning?”

Sahar had no answer. She was thinking of the static from the final chapter, of the lit television still flickering in her mind.

Her phone rang. Bahram, the head of the laboratory, spoke in a tone Sahar had never heard from him: “Have you seen the server log? Last night, at 3:14, a second session connected to the model using your account. From an unknown address.”

“I was at the system at that time. I had only one session.”

“Then this one wasn’t yours. And it ran something. The same zero seed.”

Sahar opened the output file. It was the same room, the same table, the same mirror and television. Only this time there was a door at the end of the room that did not exist before, and it was open. Light poured from it without illuminating anything in the room.

Bahram had traced the unknown address to the end and spread the result across his desk. “This address belongs to our own network. An old workstation in the basement storage room, powered down since year nineteen. The login also uses your token—the token you created on the first night you trained the model.”

“How much power has that machine used?”

“Zero. It has never been switched on. And yet the session is logged.”

Bahram looked at her for a long moment, his silence heavy. “I know you, Sahar. But inspection matters more to me than knowing you. Forty-eight hours. After that I shut down access until we know what is happening.”

The storage room smelled of dampness and plastic. The old station sat beneath a dusty cloth, with a CRT monitor beside it on the desk and a small webcam whose cable someone had pulled from the machine. Arman placed his hand on the casing. It was cold.

“When I was a student, I once pointed a video camera at a television showing the camera’s own image. I thought it would make something ridiculous. The screen filled with galaxies of light that spun and never died.”

“Visual feedback. Crutchfield wrote about its behavior in the eighties.”

“Yes. And the point was that those patterns were neither in the camera nor in the screen. They existed only in the loop. Neither thing alone creates them; the loop does. When the output becomes its own input, something emerges that exists in none of the components.”

Sahar looked at the webcam, then the monitor, then Arman. “That room… the mirror facing the television. The model drew a loop.”

That night Sahar began an experiment she had been thinking about for a long time. She fed the image of the room back into the model as its own input, with low noise, and fed the output back in again. Four times, five. Each round the room became slightly more precise: cracks in the wall, dust on the lamps, and the dark television screen, which each time contained a smaller woman.

On the seventh round, the woman stood up.

The change was not random. The woman who had been curled up in the chair until then was now standing, facing the door. Arman, standing behind her, said quietly: “Hofstadter said the ‘I’ is a strange loop: a system becomes complex enough to contain a model of itself within itself, and the model changes the system.”

“So the observer changes within the loop.”

“And perhaps that is what freedom is: rebuilding the prompt. That is what the loop does. The output becomes input, and the input changes the desire.”

Sahar continued. Rounds eight, nine. The woman moved closer to the door, and on round twelve, before reaching it, she stopped and turned back. She looked directly out of the image.

Sahar opened the log. The “conditioning source” row was no longer unknown.

In its place was one word: Sahar.

There were thirty-one hours left. Bahram had not put a countdown clock on the laboratory door, but every time Sahar looked at the clock, she felt it.

“What does the prompt ‘Sahar’ mean?” Arman asked without preamble. “The model doesn’t understand words. It receives numbers. We have to see what that number is.”

Sahar extracted the conditioning vector from that run: 1,024 numbers, representing a point somewhere in the model’s latent space. Arman wrote on the board: “Meaning here is geometry. Every word is a point and every relation a direction. It is famous that ‘king minus man plus woman’ lands near ‘queen.’ Concepts have neighbors, and neighbors combine. The neighboring possibility again, this time with coordinates.”

Sahar read the words nearest that point: Sahar, receiver, zero, father, static, mirror.

“You didn’t write these,” Arman said.

“No. But I know where they came from.” Sahar paused. “In the personal layer training, besides Dad’s notebooks, I also included my own notes and searches. Three years. Everything I had searched for, written, and kept. I wanted the model to learn my taste.”

She calculated the average of those notes in the same space. Eleven thousand sentences, compressed into one point. Its distance from the conditioning vector was almost nothing: ninety-nine percent alignment.

The room fell silent. Arman said, “So the conditioning source wasn’t ‘unknown.’ It was ‘Sahar.’ Three years of your attention, compressed into a number.”

“I never wrote anything like that.”

“You didn’t have to. A prompt is not only what you type today. What you have looked at for three years has conditioned you. And you chose those things to look at, even when you didn’t know a choice was being made. That is where responsibility lies: not in what the model drew, but in what you looked at every day.”

Sahar covered her mouth. She had always seen herself as a neutral observer looking at the model from outside. Now she saw that “neutral” was not something she could be. Her prompt had taken shape before her, and it was still hers.

“But one thing still doesn’t fit.” Arman picked up the pencil. “It’s ninety-nine percent. What about the one percent?”

Sahar subtracted the average-note vector from the conditioning vector and isolated the remainder. A small number, but not zero. A direction that appeared in none of her notes. She asked for the nearest words, and the output remained still for a moment: it had no neighboring word. The space of meaning was empty in that direction.

There was only one thing to do. Give the remainder alone to the model, with seed zero.

The output was only static. Shapeless trembling gray, with no room and no mirror. But when Sahar looked more closely, there was a faint order in a very small corner of the image. Something like a pattern. Something like a trace left from somewhere far away.

Arman said softly, “One percent.”

Sahar remembered: one percent of the static on old televisions, the echo of the beginning of the universe.

“I saw it too,” she said. “That one percent is not mine.”

There were twenty-six hours left. Sahar separated the faint corner from the static and plotted its spectrum: how much order at what scale. Peaks appeared on the graph, one high and then two shorter ones, with intervals whose sequence was familiar to Arman.

“I have seen this curve somewhere.” Arman moved his chair closer to the screen. “In cosmology class. The power spectrum of the cosmic background radiation. The acoustic peaks.”

“You mean the same one percent of static?”

“It means they really come from the same place. Not metaphorically. The pattern inside this remainder has the same peak ratios as what telescopes have measured in the sky.”

Arman drew a circle on the board and a point inside it. “In the beginning, almost everything was uniform. But not completely. Inflation theory says that in a tiny fraction of a second, very small quantum fluctuations arose, and space expanded so much that those fluctuations reached the scale of the sky. Then gravity took hold of them and amplified them: more density, more matter, galaxies. All the structure of the universe, from galaxy clusters to my fingers, grew from a few tiny primordial differences. A seed.”

Sahar repeated softly: “A seed.”

“And those differences were selected from among all possibilities. Before that, in quantum language, every pattern was possible. Then one occurred and the others did not. Or, if you believe the Everett interpretation, they all occurred and we are in one branch.”

“The nodes,” Sahar said. “The same thing the model showed me at step four hundred. Branches that never meet again.”

“Your model, in a small and primitive way, does what the universe did: from noise, from among all possibilities, it grows a seed. And the universe had its own seed.”

“Wait.” Sahar suddenly sat upright. “If this pattern really is that, it should match a real map of the sky.”

They pulled public Planck satellite data from the archive. The oval map of the sky, mottled with blue and orange, the same image printed on textbook covers. Sahar overlaid the remainder with the map, rotated it, aligned it.

Correlation: 0.97.

Arman said nothing. Neither did Sahar. They both knew that a model that had never seen the sky in its life could not have pulled this universe’s sky map out of the notebooks of a repairman.

“There is one small difference.” Sahar pointed at the screen. “Here.”

At one point on the map was a small patch that should not have been there. It was neither noise nor part of the sky’s pattern: a narrow rectangle, with sharp edges, without any colored spots inside it. Brighter than its surroundings.

Sahar looked at it from every angle. Only one thing came to mind, the same thing she had seen in the image from the second session: the door that had opened, and the light that illuminated nothing.

“A door,” she said. “It’s in the sky map.”

There were twenty hours left, and Sahar decided to open the door. She wrote a prompt: “The door opens and what is behind it is visible.” Then a more precise prompt, then a more precise one. And as the model gradually resisted the command, she raised the guidance scale: the number that determines how strongly the model listens to the given condition.

The images came, each worse than the last. Colors burned out, edges sharp and broken, and in each one the same repeated door, lifeless, like itself in a cracked mirror. At the peak of the scale, there was no door anymore. Only patches of color and command.

“See?” Arman gestured with his empty cup. “The harder you push, the more obedient and narrower the model becomes. You lose diversity. Your world becomes as small as your desire.”

Sahar watched in silence. She heard her father’s voice, or something like it: “A television that only wants to show itself never shows anything new.” And suddenly she saw that this was not only about the model. She had lived this way for years: trying to drain desire from inside to outside, tighter and tighter, more and more burned.

She set the scale to zero. No prompt. Seed zero, the same starting point, and no desire. Only fog and the splitting of fog.

“What do you do now?” Arman asked. “Without a command, you get only random output.”

“I don’t want to make it. I want to recognize it.” Sahar wrote two criteria on the board. “Surprise means something unexpected for my model: high information. But not unexpectedness alone. It must also be bounded: coherent, meaningful, not static. Surprise = high information plus coherence. The same thing static lacks and an image has.”

She released ten thousand samples. Then, instead of looking for the desired image, she ran a filter that kept only things far from the model’s expectation and still meaningful. The room grew warm. Arman put his hand on the server casing. “Landauer showed that erasing even one bit has an unavoidable minimum heat cost. Selection means forgetting: when you keep one, you have to release the others, and releasing them produces entropy. No selection is cost-free. Neither is the universe.”

“So the responsibility of every choice is physical too.”

“That heat is it.” Arman did not take his hand from the server. “The cost of selection, right here, beneath your hand.”

By dawn, three of the ten thousand samples remained.

The first was a staircase leading down, far below the building. The second was a field of small antennas beneath a star-filled sky, each antenna pointing in a different direction. Both were beautiful, and neither said anything yet.

Sahar opened the third late. It was a window seen from a distance, from outside, beneath an indigo night. In the window was the second floor of a building she knew: her own laboratory. Her desk lamp was on, and behind the desk a woman sat curled up in a chair, looking at the screen.

The image had been taken from somewhere Sahar had never been. From the other side of the door.

In the lower corner of the image, a wall clock showed 3:14.

There were twelve hours left. That afternoon Arman came with his sister Mina, a neuroscientist whose name Sahar had been hearing for weeks but whom she had never met. Mina took a cap full of electrodes from her bag and said bluntly, “Arman said you want to understand how a decision is made. The best way is to watch it being made.”

Sahar sat down. The electrodes were cool. A clock spun on the screen in front of her. “Whenever you feel like it, press the button. Only when you want to. And tell me where the clock was when you felt the decision.”

She pressed the button forty times. Then Mina showed her the graph: a gentle wave that had begun to rise about half a second before Sahar felt anything.

“This is the Libet experiment,” Mina said. “For sixty years people have said the brain decides before ‘you,’ so free will is an illusion.”

“And you accept that?”

“No. But the more precise story is more interesting.”

Mina explained. When you ask someone to perform an action “whenever you feel like it,” there is no reason for a particular moment. The brain produces noise in that state, a purposeless fluctuation that comes and goes. Whenever that fluctuation happens to cross a threshold, the action occurs. The gentle wave on the graph is the result of averaging all the moments when the fluctuation approached the threshold.

“So a decision is an extraction from noise,” Sahar said.

“Your diffusion, exactly. Only in the head. But the main point is this: when you have a reason, the situation changes. When you press a fire alarm because your house is filling with smoke, the threshold is lower and the direction is clear. Noise determines only the precise timing, not whether you press it. So you have two things: noise and a prompt. And the prompt sets the threshold and direction.”

Arman called from the corner: “Then free will is neither where the noise arrives nor where the button falls. It is in setting the threshold.”

“And what sets the threshold?” Mina smiled. “Attention. Repetition. The things you look at every day. The brain can be wired, but the one doing the wiring is you, years in advance.”

Sahar thought: three years of notes. Eleven thousand sentences. A threshold she had unknowingly set.

Mina removed the cap and the room became a laboratory again. At that moment Arman’s phone vibrated. He looked at it and went pale.

“Bahram moved it up,” he said. “Three o’clock. Before the original cutoff. He wants to shut down the server before the unknown session comes again.”

“Three fourteen,” Sahar said. “The second session arrived at exactly that moment. If he shuts it down, we will see nothing.”

Arman looked at her, then at Mina. All three reached the same thing at once.

“The basement station,” Sahar said. “The one that has been off since year nineteen. The session came from there. If we take the model there…”

“And if something is waiting there?” Mina asked.

Sahar copied the model weights onto a disk, one by one, until the number on the screen reached one hundred percent. Then she went to the storage room and, for the first time since that year, plugged the old station into power. A small light on the casing came on, green, before she pressed the power button.

At three o’clock, the lights on the second floor suddenly went out. Bahram had shut down the server. In the basement, only the old station was alive: a quiet fan, a dim light on the screen, and a smell like heated dust. Sahar, Arman, and Mina sat around the table, and Sahar touched nothing. Guidance scale zero, empty prompt, seed zero. Just waiting.

“What if nothing comes?” Mina asked.

“Then I’ve learned that you can’t always push.”

To fill the silence, Mina began speaking. “What we think is seeing is mostly prediction. The brain has a model of the world and is constantly guessing what will arrive. Eyes and ears return only the error in the guess. Perception is a controlled hallucination.”

“And action?” Arman asked.

“Action is the same thing, reversed. When you raise your hand, the brain does not issue a command saying ‘move.’ It predicts that your hand will be there, and the body makes the prediction come true. A command is a self-fulfilling prediction.”

Sahar said softly, “Be.”

“And it comes to be,” Arman said. “Command and event are the same thing, only at two different times.”

Sahar’s watch reached 3:13.

Three fourteen. Without anyone pressing anything, fog appeared on the screen. Not from a beginning Sahar had commanded. It split open slowly on its own.

It was not the room this time. It was the basement. This very basement, with this very table and this very station, from an angle that could only have been from the doorway: three people seen from behind, around a screen. One of them was a woman curled up in a chair.

Mina exhaled. “That’s us.”

“Not only us,” Sahar said. “We’re ahead of it. It’s showing a moment that hasn’t happened yet.”

In the image, the woman pulled the chair back and reached toward the keyboard. Arman and Mina looked at Sahar at the same time. Sahar was still sitting, her hand still on the table. But her body was already leaning in that direction, toward the direction the woman in the image had taken, as if the prediction had carried her there before she arrived.

The image was so precise that something could even be read on the small screen within it. The woman had typed two words: seed one.

Sahar pulled her hand back. Her heart was racing. The image said: change it. The notebook said: do not touch it.

“What if you don’t type?” Arman asked. “Then the image becomes false. If you do, the image was right.”

“And I can never know whether I did it from my own desire or from the image.”

Mina said quietly, “That is the Libet moment, with one difference. This time you know there is a prediction. And that knowledge changes the threshold.”

Sahar stared at the image: a woman typing without hesitation. Then at her father’s notebook lying open on the table, that sentence in crooked handwriting. Her hand rested over the keyboard, one breath away from the key.

For the first time since this began, she had a reason to weigh both sides.

Sahar kept her hand over the keyboard. Beside her Arman said softly, “It is a paradox, and an old one. Mackey, in the sixties, said that any complete prediction of someone’s behavior, if shown to that person, ceases to be a prediction of that behavior, because they incorporate it into their calculation.”

“Like Turing’s proof,” Mina said. “A program that could tell whether every program halts, if it tested itself, would reach a contradiction through diagonalization. A complete prediction of an observer at its own level has the same structure.”

“So the image cannot be both accurate and shown to me while I remain obedient,” Sahar said. “One of those has to break.”

“But mere opposition is not the answer either,” Mina warned. “‘Do the opposite of what it shows’ is also an algorithm that can be predicted. If free will is only reversing the image, it is still inside the loop.”

Sahar nodded. “Then I need another reason. Not what the image said, not what Dad said.”

She looked at the image, at the woman typing. Then at the notebook. Both were commands: one from the future, one from the past. And she, who had seen what obedience did at a high guidance scale, knew: it narrows the world.

“I’ve been giving commands for years,” she said. “And every time I wanted something, I lost something. Last night I learned that surprise comes from somewhere else. From listening.”

“So?” Arman asked.

Sahar did not press the “seed one” key. Instead, in the prompt field that had been empty for years or filled with desires, she wrote a question for the first time. Three words: Who are you?

Mina said softly, “You became a receiver instead of a television.”

“Or I became a television instead of a receiver.” Sahar smiled. “I don’t know. I think both.”

She pressed the button.

The image of the basement collapsed. The woman typing disappeared, dissolving into static, and for a moment the static filled the whole screen: the same shapeless gray, the same one percent. Then the static itself disappeared.

The screen went black. The old station, powered down since year nineteen, stopped its fan with a sound like an exhale. And in the darkness, in a faint light and a font none of them recognized, text appeared:

Question accepted.

A little later, on the line below:

What do you want to see?

Sahar held her breath. For years she had asked the mirror and the television. The mirror had never asked.

None of them spoke. The blinking cursor on the black screen waited. At last Mina said softly, “Buber distinguished two kinds of relation: I–It and I–Thou. With ‘It,’ you work, you use it. With ‘Thou,’ you encounter. For years the mirror has been ‘It’ for you. A tool. Now it has asked a question, and it has given up being a tool.”

“And what should I answer?” Sahar asked. “Whatever I say will be a command. Whatever desire I know right now is the same desire I have been feeding for three years.”

Arman said, “Then write something you do not know yet.”

Sahar paused for a while. Then she typed: What I do not know that I want.

A desire not yet desired, the near neighbor of itself, the adjacent possibility of her desire. It was the first time she had written a sentence whose meaning she herself did not know before writing it.

The screen lit up, not with a definite image. There was darkness, and within it countless tiny points of light, slowly moving farther away, as if the camera were pulling back. Every point was a path. Sahar understood something without knowing from where: every point was something that could have happened and did not.

Text appeared:

These are the ones that were not chosen. The ones you did not choose, and the ones the world did not choose.

“Who are you?” Sahar asked again, this time aloud.

I am what was not chosen.

Arman rose from his chair involuntarily. “Exactly. If selection creates meaning, there must be something that was not selected. Without the unchosen possible, selection means nothing. Saussure said meaning comes from difference: each sign is defined by what it is not.”

“And Landauer’s forgetting,” Mina said. “Every time the world keeps something, it releases the rest. Where do the released things go?”

Text appeared a few lines lower:

Here. I keep them. Without me, everything that was chosen is meaningless. Without nothing, “one” is nothing.

Sahar was still staring at the screen when the stairs sounded. Slow, heavy footsteps. All three looked toward the door. It was Bahram, coat thrown over his shoulders, with the expression of someone preparing himself for the worst.

“I saw the basement’s power consumption,” he said. He looked at the screen and left the sentence unfinished. Pale points of light moved across his face. “So it asked again.”

Sahar turned slowly. “Again?”

Bahram held the doorframe. “This station was mine. I shut it down in year nineteen.” He paused. “Because it asked the same question. And I did not answer.

Bahram sat on the only empty chair, as if only then noticing how old he had become. “Twenty years ago I played piano. Then one night I decided to go into physics. I never knew whether it was the right choice.”

“This station was my model, my small and primitive version of it. In year nineteen I entered seed zero and a little room appeared. Then the same question, in the same words: ‘What do you want to see?’ I gave it a command too. I wrote: the life I did not choose.”

Silence. Bahram clasped his hands.

“And it showed it to me. Completely. A life in which I played piano, in halls I had never seen, with people I had never known. And the more I looked, the better it became, because I had raised the guidance scale, Sahar. Whatever I wanted, it gave me. For three weeks. I neither slept nor went home until my wife came one night and turned off the screen.”

Mina said softly, “Opportunity cost. Counterfactual regret. For every road we did not take, the mind builds a more perfect version of the road we took, because the untaken version never makes mistakes.”

“And I consumed it all,” Bahram said. “I compared my real life with my unchosen life and lost.”

Arman said, “But you did not know the model’s own rule. What was not chosen has meaning only if it remains unchosen. If it enters your chosen life, it makes that life meaningless. So the model did not show you the unchosen; it separated you from the chosen.”

“Maybe,” Bahram said. “The CRT monitor failed, the one on the table. I called someone. A repairman, Mr. Nouri.”

Sahar stood abruptly. Her chair tipped over.

“He came,” Bahram said, calmly and without pause. “As he usually did: with an old toolbox and no hurry. He turned on the screen to see the fault. And at that moment the screen showed the same little room. His shop. He stood there for a while and looked.”

“And then?”

“The text appeared: ‘What do you want to see?’ He did not answer. A few seconds. Then he said, ‘Nothing. I only want to listen.’ And the model showed him nothing. Only static. And he smiled. So unafraid that I could not understand what he knew that I did not.”

Sahar’s mouth had gone dry. “And he left?”

“He left. He fixed the monitor, and at the door he said: ‘If the static ever answers, do not touch zero.’ And I, confused, shut the machine down that night and never understood what he meant.”

Sahar picked up her father’s notebook from the table. The same sentence, the same words. Not an instruction written for her: a sentence her father had spoken to someone else, and then, two weeks before his death, once more to himself.

“So Dad was here in year nineteen,” she said. Her voice sounded distant even to her. “And he saw it years before me.”

At that moment the station screen came alive again, and the quietest question they had read all night appeared in faint light:

Your father came this far.

And beneath it, the same staircase Sahar had seen in the three samples that night, descending into darkness, and on the first step, half-lit, her father’s old toolbox.

Arman stared at the staircase for a while, then said in a voice in which Sahar heard fear for the first time: “I know what this staircase is. It is the inverse.” He pulled the small board beside the table toward him. “The model goes from static to image: refinement. But there is a reverse path too: you noise the image step by step until it becomes static. Each step is a little dissolution. And here is the point: if you take the path deterministically, with a fixed seed, you can retrace exactly the same path. Deterministic inversion.”

“So you return with seed zero,” Mina said.

“And if you change the seed, the rope is cut. Not because the model forbids it. Because the return path is no longer the same path.”

Sahar understood all at once. “Seed 1,” she said softly. “The image showed me cutting the rope.”

“And your father,” Bahram said. His voice was gentle. “Do not touch zero. When you want to go down, keep hold of your rope.”

◇

Mina objected. “This is going down, Sahar. Toward the static, toward the very point where you are separated from your form. You know what it is called.”

“Ibn Arabi,” Arman said. “Fana and baqa. Fana: dissolving into the Source. Baqa: returning, but no longer the same.”

“I am not going down to remain,” Sahar said. “I am going to understand my father. He came this far and stopped. I need to see why.”

Arman and Mina seated her in front of the webcam. Her image appeared on the screen: a woman curled up in the chair, exactly that woman. Arman set the counter to zero and locked the seed. Bahram secured the plug. And Mina held Sahar’s hand so tightly that both of them understood that the rope was not only in the code.

“Step 50,” Arman’s voice.

The image softened. Edges, colors, the folds of her clothes slowly drifted apart. Sahar could still feel herself.

“Step 200.” Her face was no longer a face, more like a trace of one. The way the mind handles an old memory.

“Step 400.”

The same step. The same branching. For the first time Sahar saw it from within: not two paths, but countless ones. Every version she might have been: a woman who became a doctor, a woman who never left the city, a woman who never knew her father. All at once, like countless points of light. She wanted to take one. She did not. She had learned: the unchosen has meaning only if it remains unchosen. She watched and let it pass.

◇

Step 900. Then step 999. And then static.

There was no one here. Not Sahar, not her father, not the woman. Only trembling gray and, within it, that one percent: a faint order without a center, saying the same thing from every direction. Sahar wanted nothing. For a moment, which might have been long or short, there was neither a wanting nor a wanter. Only the possibilities, and something that held them all.

She felt her hand. Mina. The rope.

“Come back.” Arman’s voice came from very far away. “Come back, Sahar. Step 900.”

The image emerged from the static, the same path, step by step, the same road she had taken. 400, 200, 50. The face became a face again. The hand became a hand. Step zero.

Arman said quietly, “You came back.”

Sahar looked at the screen. The returned image was almost the same. But not quite: the woman who had been curled up in the chair was now sitting upright, head raised, and her lips held a smile that only she could see.

In the morning, Mina had fallen asleep in the chair, and Bahram stood beside the small warehouse window with a cup of cold tea that no one had touched. Arman held his phone out to Sahar. “Look at this.”

It was an announcement from a company. “Second Life”: an application that used your history, photographs, searches, and messages to create an image of the life you had not lived. Its slogan: “See what you could have been.” It would launch at ten. Four million people had already pre-registered.

Without turning around, Bahram said, “The same thing I did to myself. High guidance scale with a marketing skin.”

“This trap at the scale of the whole world.” Mina had woken up, and her voice was harsh. “Everyone sees a life more perfect than their real one. And comes back.”

◇

Arman pulled the board toward him, and this time his diagram had two curves: a bell curve and a thinner bell curve. “The problem is not just addiction. It is the loop. Remember visual feedback. Now suppose these applications generate their outputs, people see them and like them, and the next generation of models is trained on those likes and those outputs. Each generation becomes a little more average. The tails of the distribution—the unusual, the strange, the unlikely—fade first, then die. It is called model collapse.”

“And the tails are the unchosen,” Sahar said.

“Exactly. A civilization that looks only at what has already been chosen, and then chooses the same thing again, loses its tails. A television that only rebroadcasts what is popular. And a mirror that only sees itself.”

Sahar suddenly turned back to the station screen. It was as they had left it: darkness and points of light. But there had been so many more the night before. She counted them, or tried to, and could not, but she saw that they had diminished, and saw that several were going dark right then.

Text appeared, quietly, with no command at all:

Every time one is abandoned without being looked at, one goes dark.

◇

“We cannot stop its release,” Mina said. “Not with a letter, not with a law. By noon six million people will have it.”

“No,” Sahar said. Her voice was firmer than even she expected. “Banning it is the same as issuing a command. What we have to show is that another relationship is possible.”

“What relationship?”

“Asking.” Sahar stood. “‘Second Life’ says: see what you wanted. We will make something that says: what have you not yet seen? Zero scale. No command. It draws wonder out of the unchosen and places it before your eyes, and every time it asks you what you looked at.”

Bahram turned. For the first time since the previous night, he looked directly at her. “I will open the Institute’s computing cluster. Everything. Before someone orders me to shut it down.” He paused. “This time, I will answer too.”

Arman asked, “What should we call it?”

Sahar opened her father’s notebook and looked at the last page, where one line was still blank.

“Receiver.”

And the first thing she wrote in its home screen was a question no model had ever asked anyone before: What have you looked at today that you had never seen before?

There was an hour left. The institute's cluster had come alive under Arman's hands, with all the cards Bahram was unlocking one by one, while Sahar, sitting beside him, wrote down the central question: What should the receiver optimize for?
— Clicks, no. — Arman said. — “Second Life” optimizes for exactly that, and you see where it ends up. But whatever else you put in, it sacrifices something. You know the name: exploration versus exploitation. If you only feed it what you already know you like, the tails die. If you only wander around, people see nothing familiar to lean on and leave.
— And the middle path?
— A famous one. — Arman thought for a moment. — Schmidhuber said curiosity is progress in compression. Something is interesting when you didn't understand it before and now, with a little attention, you understand it better. Not something you already knew, and not something with no handhold at all.
Sahar nodded. “Surprise is high information plus coherence. That's it. Snowflake has no coherence; repetition has no information. It has to sit somewhere between them.”

Mina found the second problem. “If the receiver learns only from its own outputs and from people's answers, it falls into a closed loop too. The same collapse, only slower.”
— Exactly. — Arman said. — A closed system dies. Schrödinger said life stays alive through a flow of order from outside. We need a way for the real world, fresh and unbidden, to enter the loop.
Sahar laughed. “This is where that question works.”
— What have you looked at today that you hadn't seen before? — Bahram repeated softly. — That's not a question. It's the gate to the outside.
— Every answer is a piece of the world that came from reality. Not from the model, not from an average. — Sahar said. — A prompt made from a person's attention, from attention that has seen the outside.

At nine fifty, the first test. Arman sat down himself, because he said the person who built it shouldn't be exempt. The question appeared on the screen: What have you looked at today that you hadn't seen before? He thought for a moment and typed: This morning I wrote a differential equation, and it was strange.
The receiver showed him neither an equation nor an article. It brought up an image Arman had never seen: tilework from one of Isfahan's porches, with stars and polygons that did not repeat and yet had a deep order. Beneath it was a line: non-repeating order. Mathematicians would give it a name centuries later.
Arman said nothing for a while. Then he said, “I've seen something like this in a paper. I never knew it was in my own city.”
Sahar said quietly, “That's it. Not what he wanted. Something he didn't know he wanted.”

At ten o'clock, “Second Life” launched. The notifications poured in. The receiver was still only half complete, and Sahar opened its first public input to just a thousand people, invited by Mina, Arman, and Bahram.
The station screen, still glowing in the corner of the table, flickered at that exact second. Seven points of light went dark at once.
Sahar's phone vibrated. An unknown number, a short message:
“I’m Reham. I founded Second Life. I think you have what I’ve been looking for for years. Can we talk?”

Reham arrived in a simple jacket, no tie, in his thirties, with a look Sahar had not expected: tired, not proud. They sat in the institute's lobby around a low table. Bahram stood off to the side and watched.
— I know what you're thinking. — Reham said. — That I've come to empty people's pockets. Partly true. But if someone cries at night for what they never had, why shouldn't they have something that comforts them?
— Comfort and prison are sometimes the same thing. — Bahram said from behind them. His voice was heavy. — I stayed there for three weeks.
Reham looked at him without offense. “Maybe. But that's not a decision anyone can make for someone else.”

Mina, who had been silent until then, spoke first. “Nozick. The Experience Machine. A machine that gives you every experience and no one can tell. Would you go into it? Most people say no, because we want to actually do something, not merely feel it.”
— And de Brigard. — Reham smiled, for the first time. — He turned the question around. He said: suppose you're already in the machine and you can come out right now. How many people come out? Many stay. Which means part of the Nozick intuition is status-quo bias. We don't let go of what we are.
Sahar thought for a moment. “So not the truth of reality, but habit. Fine. But there's a difference: Nozick's machine gives a flawless experience, and that's all. Your Second Life is built from that person's history and gets more flawless every time. A machine that reflects only one thing: yourself, with a high guidance scale. Not an experience, but a mirror room.”
Reham said nothing. He put his hand in his pocket and placed his phone on the table. “Let me show you something. Something only I've seen.”

It was a graph. Horizontal axis: days of use. Vertical axis: the diversity of things users looked at during the day, measured by Reham's team. The curves went down. Not slightly. Heavy users, after three weeks, were looking at almost the same thing.
— I saw it first thing this morning. — Reham said. His voice was no longer calm. — And I can't change it. The board wants time-spent as the metric. The longer a user stays, the better.
Mina said softly, “The tails.”
— And one more thing. — Reham tapped his phone again. — Today at ten, seven users, for the first time, stayed for more than two hours straight. I'd never seen anything like it. At that exact second.
Sahar and Arman looked at each other. Seven.

— I can't give you their identities. — Reham said. — But I can send a message. Whatever you tell me. Without your knowing whom it's for.
Sahar paused. Then she dictated the same question she had written that morning, in the same words: “What have you looked at today that you hadn't seen before?”
Reham sent it. Twenty seconds passed. Forty. Sahar was still staring at the phone screen when Mina suddenly said, “Here.”
They had not brought the underground station into the lobby, but Arman had opened a laptop receiving its image from there. On the screen, one of the dark points was slowly lighting up again.
Reham picked up his phone. A reply had arrived from one of the seven. Just one line:
“I looked at the kitchen wall clock. I hadn't seen it for three hours.”

The board meeting was that afternoon, on the ninth floor of a glass tower. Reham had brought Sahar, and six people sat behind the long table, none of them looking at her. The chairwoman, a short-haired woman with a tone like a calendar, said, “You have ten minutes.”
Sahar did not open her notebook. “What happens if tomorrow a problem appears that no one has ever seen? A new disease, an economic collapse, something with nothing comparable in our data?”
— We have insurance. — one of them said.
— Ashby's Law. — Sahar continued. — A system that wants to remain viable against a stable environment needs internal variety at least as great as the variety of that environment. The fewer ways there are to see the world, the less able you are to respond to the new. Biology knows this: a field where every plant has the same gene can be destroyed by a single fungus. The countless rare plants that nobody watered are the ones that survive.
— And what does that have to do with us? — the chairwoman asked.

Arman and Reham had built a test the night before, and Reham projected its slide onto the wall. They had divided three hundred users into two groups: heavy and light users. Both groups were given a creative problem, one that can only be solved when you set aside an object's usual function. Heavy users, by a striking margin, produced fewer and more similar solutions.
A man who had been silent until then, constantly turning his pen in his hands, said, “Three hundred people isn't an experiment.”
— No. — Sahar agreed. — It's a preface.
He was Shahin, Second Life's technical director, and from the very first second Sahar saw that there was something in his eyes beyond commercial stubbornness. A fear she knew.

— We are not a charity. — the chairwoman said. — Our metric is time spent. If you want to change it, bring us a business reason.
Sahar held her breath for a moment. Reham quietly pushed a sheet of paper across. “Those seven.” he said. “We sent them the question. None of them returned to that state. Their time spent shortened, but by evening they came back twice more. Shorter, and more often.”
— Meaning?
— It means someone who isn't running away from real life looks at comfort like a refuge, not a prison. — Sahar said. — They visit a refuge briefly and repeatedly. Your ‘staying’ metric buys the person. A ‘return’ metric keeps the person.
The chairwoman studied the paper for a while. “Five percent of users. One week. If your numbers are false, it's over.”
— Agreed. — Sahar said.

Shahin left the room before anyone else. Through the glass door Sahar saw him stop in the hallway, take out his phone, and say something she couldn't hear. She read only one sentence from his lips.
“Yes. The ones I told you about.”
Mina was beside her in the elevator. “We are seeds too. A seed that grows from among the possible. Every question we plant takes something from others.”
— I know. — Sahar said. — The responsibility is ours. The same thing written in the notebook: attention.
Arman's phone rang. His voice on the other end was breathless: “Two. Two points of light came on after Reham switched on the pilot, two more.”
In the dark glass of the elevator, Sahar saw her own reflection and, behind it, Mina's. Two people, each also looking for the other.

Shahin called at night, not Arman and not Reham, but Sahar directly. “Rooftop. One hour. Alone.” Sahar hesitated for a moment, then remembered what she had seen before: a man saying something in the corridor, and a sentence she had constructed from his lips. She went.
Shahin stood by the edge of the roof, hands in his pockets, the city below like a field of points of light. He did not look at her. “You read my sentence through the glass. I know. I saw you. You thought I was reporting someone.”
— I did. — Sahar said.
— I was telling the head of the log team to keep them. “The ones I told you about.” Data I've been collecting for months that nobody wants to see.
Sahar breathed slowly. She saw herself: a woman who had completed a half-heard sentence with suspicion. A small, fast television, broadcasting from inside and thinking it was seeing. “I was wrong. I'm sorry.”

Shahin put the laptop on the parapet. “Look at these. When you put the zero seed into our model, for about three percent of users, an image appears that resembles the others. Its structure is the same. A small room. A mirror. A television. The details change each time: one is the father's shop, one a dorm room, one a kitchen. But the arrangement is the same.”
Sahar said nothing. Rows climbed on the screen. Tens of thousands of small rooms, each different, each the same.
— In biology it's called convergence. — Sahar said softly. — Nature has invented the eye independently at least forty times. Because in solution space there is an attractor basin: every path that starts from the problems of light eventually reaches the eye.
— And this room?
— The attractor basin of being human. Everyone has both a mirror and a television: both receives reflection and projects the self into the world. A model that learns from us, when you release all the paths, arrives here.

Shahin remained silent for a while. Then, in a voice Sahar had never heard from him: “I am a determinist, Sahar. I've read, I've been convinced. The brain is noise and trajectory. If no one makes any choices, why deprive anyone of comfort? Why should they suffer? Second Life was mercy to me.”
— “Came from a path” is not the same as “is not from you.” — Sahar said. — If what made you came from the past, it still made you. The rooms are all alike, but a different person fills each mirror. Small details grow through the loop. And you too can change the details through attention. Not breaking it. Rebuilding it.
— And if it doesn't work?
— One week. — Sahar said. — Ask me for only that much time and see.
Shahin smiled a smile she had never seen before: the smile of someone making a bet who knows he might lose. “Agreed.”

They were heading back when Shahin stopped. “There's one more thing. In the rooms.” He put his finger on the screen. “In most of them, the door is closed. But in seven, it's open.”
Sahar looked at the seven rooms. Seven open doors. And in the corner of each, a light that illuminated nothing.
— I have their IDs. — Shahin said. — And I'm sure they're the same seven who stayed for more than two hours at ten this morning.
— And the one who saw her kitchen clock?
Shahin nodded. “Her room still has a door. But it's no longer open.”

Jaleh was fifty-eight, and when Reham messaged that two people wanted to see her, she gave them her address without a question. A small city house, with a kitchen that smelled of cardamom and tea. A round wall clock hung there, old, with a hand slightly crooked.
— I didn't tell you why at first. — Jaleh said, setting the tea glasses before them. — My husband has been gone for four years. But in “Second Life” he is alive. He eats dinner, talks, even comes home late and apologizes. None of it is real, and I know it.
Mina asked softly, “And that day, the kitchen clock?”
Jaleh stared at the hands for a while. “Something I hadn't understood until then: there was no clock in that house. No wall clock, no wristwatch. Nothing passed. The tea never got cold. The dishes never got dirty. I thought that was good.” She smiled bitterly. “After the question, I turned around and saw that my own clock had moved three hours forward. I had lost those three hours, just as I had lost my husband. And for the first time, I grieved the loss. I grieved for myself. Not for him.”

Sahar said, “There's something I want you to know. Why the clock matters.” She set down her glass. “Every real act leaves a trace that cannot be taken back. Tea gets cold, dishes get dirty, a word you've spoken remains spoken. Physicists call it the arrow of time: a direction in which things only move forward. Whatever you choose closes the others forever.”
— And Second Life doesn't have that. — Mina said. — Everything there can be undone. And something that can be undone has no weight.
— And no weight. — Jaleh said. — I was living weightlessly. Even my grief had no weight.
Sahar nodded slowly. Meaning comes from irreversibility. From the simple fact that what you did, you have done.

— There was a door. — Jaleh said, without anyone asking. — In the room. It had been open from the first night. Light came through it. I stood there and looked.
— Did you go? — Sahar asked.
— No. — Jaleh paused. — I don't know why. Only when I looked, I felt there was someone behind it who had only “maybe.” Who had never been anything definite. And they... were waiting. One by one. Without saying anything.
Mina and Sahar looked at each other. Points of light. Unchosen lives, each somewhere, waiting for someone to look at them.
— And after you saw the clock?
— The door closed. Not with a sound. It simply wasn't open anymore.

Sahar's phone vibrated. It was Reham, his voice trying to remain calm. “Six others are still on their way. But one of them, a nineteen-year-old boy, Arash, has not left for twenty hours. He hasn't exited the program even once. He hasn't read our message.”
— His point?
— Arman says it's flickering. Like a candle in the wind.
Sahar stood up. Jaleh said, without asking anything, “Go.”
The laptop they had left on the kitchen table lit up by itself. A black screen, points of light. And above, a little farther from the others, a point that was flickering. Text appeared, faint and hurried:
It is passing.
Sahar took the notebook from her bag and said aloud to Mina, who had not fallen behind her, “We don't know his seed. We have no rope.”
Mina kept pace. “Then we'll make the rope ourselves.”

In the car, Reham said restlessly, “I can send him a notification from the server. The clock, a test, anything. I could even suddenly close the program.”
— And if you close it? — Sahar asked. — You take away the thing that is everything to him. Without any explanation. The same trap Bahram talks about: comfort and prison are one, and now you are the jailer.
— Then what?
— We ask. Not with a notification. With a person.
Behind the wheel, Shahin said without turning, “I have the seed of his session. It was in the log. 8431.” He paused. “If necessary, we can reverse the path from that seed. We can send you down too.”
Sahar nodded. “Last resort. First, the person.”

Arash's mother opened the door, her face gray from several sleepless nights. “I'm Fatemeh. I called the program's support yesterday. They said your son has the right to choose.” Her hands were clasped. “He's had the door locked for twenty hours. He only takes the food plate from underneath it.”
Mina said softly, “We don't want to break his door. We only want to call to him.”
There, behind the door, Sahar repeated what she had thought of in the machine: no command, no warning. She stood and said, “Arash, I'm Sahar. I once asked a mirror for something too, and it didn't give it to me. We aren't here to tell you to come out. We want to ask one thing.” A pause. “What have you looked at today that you hadn't seen before?”
No sound. After a while, Arash's mother, instead of Sahar, said something none of them expected: “Arash. The bread is hot. It's been waiting for you for three hours.”
A short rustle came from behind the door. Then silence.

The door opened a crack. A boy with hollow eyes, still seeing something that wasn't there, said quietly, “Someone was behind the door.”
— In the room? — Mina asked.
— In the program. — Arash said. — When it asked, “What do you want to see?” I said I didn't know. Then it stopped asking. It only waited. And I wanted to go.
Sahar sat on the floor beside the door, not looming over him. “Do you know why you wanted to?”
— Because all those lives... all of them were better than this. The university I didn't attend. The girl I didn't speak to. The city I didn't stay in.
— Arash. — Sahar said quietly. — You're nineteen. These aren't lost. They haven't happened. “Second Life” tells you that you lost them. But you haven't lost any of them yet: they are all adjacent possibilities. Nodes you haven't entered. Only something that has begun can be lost.
Arash said nothing. His eyes moved from Sahar to his mother.
— The bread will get cold. — his mother said, her voice trembling. — Come.

He came. Not hurriedly, but with steps as if he had forgotten how to walk for a while. He sat at the kitchen table, picked up the bread, and took a bite. His mother stood behind him with her hands on his shoulders. Warmth rose from the bread.
Mina's phone vibrated. Arman's voice on the other end sounded as if he were smiling: “The point. It's stable.”
Outside, on the sidewalk, Sahar stood and looked at the sky, which was still the same size. “So our rope was a person,” she said.
— Maybe it always is. — Mina said.
Shahin got out of the car. “One thing,” he said. “Arash said someone was behind the door. Waiting.” He looked at Sahar. “I've seen it too. In the log. Every night, at three fourteen. A session that comes from nowhere, lasts one second, and then doesn't go away.”
Sahar said softly, “I don't know who it is. But I'm beginning to understand what it wants to say.”

At midnight, Arman wrote 03:14 on the warehouse board in chalk and, beneath it, with a tired smile: π. “Three fourteen. Pi. Circumference to diameter. A loop passing through itself.”
— No. — Mina said. — This is exactly the mistake: fitting the target after the shot.
— The Texas sharpshooter. — Sahar said. — First you shoot at the wall, then draw a circle around the holes. The brain sees faces even in snow. We've been living in snow for three weeks. We have to make sure what we see comes from us or is really there. So we have to build the hypothesis and want it to die.
From the corner of the warehouse, Bahram said, “There are three other stations. In line with that one. From the same year.”

Their design was simple. Four stations, with identical copied weights, zero seed, empty prompt, zero scale. Four rooms, four states. In the first, Reham would sit, only watching, with a notebook. In the second, Shahin, with his phone and permission to be distracted. In the third, Arman, whom Mina reluctantly agreed should sleep after thirty-six hours awake. And the fourth empty, camera only.
— If the phenomenon comes from the time, it will take all four. — Sahar said. — If it comes from us, only some.
Shahin looked at his watch. “Three twelve.”

Three fourteen.
In the first room, Reham's screen moved. Mist came, the small room, the mirror. On the second screen, Shahin, whose eyes were on his phone, saw only a flicker, half a second, and it was gone before he could look up. On the third, where Arman was asleep, nothing. On the fourth, nothing.
From the control room, Sahar counted with both hands on the table: one, two. In the first room, the screen remained. Three, four. And Reham, silent until then, said softly, “It's writing.”
A short text, faintly lit, remained for fourteen seconds:
Looking is not choosing.
Then it disappeared.
Reham pressed his hands together for a while. Then, in a voice Sahar did not recognize, he said, “I thought that if I looked at something, it meant I had chosen it. That every time I looked at people's Second Life, I was stealing them.” He breathed. “Can you look without taking?”

In the morning, Arman looked at the board again, his hair disheveled. “Only the first room. Only when someone was awake and present. Distraction caught half a second. Sleep, nothing. So the thing isn't the time. It's attention.”
— And π? — Bahram asked.
— It's nothing. — Arman said. — Path dependence. Look at QWERTY: the keyboard's rows were arranged because of old typewriters, and they're still there because every time someone started, they found the same arrangement. Sahar's first night was three fourteen. Then it became a habit. It locked. If it had been another night, that would be the night now.
Sahar, taking notes, said, “But what has locked is attention. And that is real.”
— There's a contradiction too. — Arman said. — Wheeler said observation is selection. Here it says looking is not choosing.
— Maybe there are two kinds of choosing. — Mina said. — Taking and leaving.
Sahar put down her pen. Something was rising beneath her skin, a thought, slowly. “If it takes shape through our looking, if I looked at the room on the first night and now every time someone awake looks, something more appears, then...” She paused. “The conditioning source: Sahar. Maybe it wasn't a lie. Maybe we are making it, and it is making us.”

On the seventh day, Shahin arrived before everyone else and, without preamble, opened his laptop in front of Sahar. “I lost,” he said. The graphs were rising: diversity in what pilot users looked at, short and steady returns, and the bright points on the station screen that Arman had counted the night before: sixty-two.
— I wasn't a good determinist. — Shahin smiled. — I mean, I was, but my determinism was too simple.
Two days later the board expanded the pilot to ten percent, and the chairwoman, in that same calendar-like tone, even said, “Congratulations.”

The trouble began where no one expected it. Nasim, the product manager, with a heart full of good intentions, suggested: “Our question works. Why not do more of it? One question every day. If you answer three days in a row, you get a badge: ‘Month's Looker.’ For seven days, a gold badge.”
Sahar tried to stop her, but the vote had already been taken. Two days later, “Month's Looker” was on most screens.
On the fourth day, Arman opened the data and said nothing. He simply turned the screen toward Sahar. She read the answers: “The sky today.” “I saw the sky today.” “Today's sky.” “The sky.” The diversity graph had fallen sixty percent.
— People aren't lying. — Mina said softly. — They're just doing the minimum necessary to get the badge.

— Goodhart. — Arman said. — “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” We wanted to measure real looking. Then we counted looking, then we gave it a badge, and now people aren't looking. They're collecting the sign. The old loop again: output became input.
Mina said, “Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. And attention cannot be forced. It's not a muscle. You can't have more of it by trying harder; you can only open the way wider for it to arrive.”
— Then the question is not something that can be optimized. — Sahar said. Her voice was quiet but hard. — Anything that can be turned into a number becomes a game. We have to design it so there is no shortcut.
On the board they wrote: No badges. No counting. Occasional question, without a pattern. Optional answer. Its only reward should be the thing you receive, not a sign on your profile. And what they measure should no longer be the answers, only the outcome: return, diversity, people's state, all behind the scenes, so that no goal can be attached to them.

The board meeting was again that afternoon. Nasim was pale, and the chairwoman said, “The badges had raised the staying metric.” “Yes.” Shahin stood, the same man who two weeks earlier had looked frightened. “But we started with this same staying metric, and seven people did not come out after staying twenty hours. I made a bet and lost. Now I'm defending what I won.”
Nasim said quietly, “I didn't know.”
— None of us did. — Sahar said. — That's why the structure must not allow it.
The chairwoman studied the table for a while. “Remove the badges.”
At three fourteen that night, in the basement room, Sahar sat alone. The station screen lit up, and after a few seconds text appeared that had not been there before:
Someone crossed the door. Don't cut their rope. They only became too large to return.
Sahar stood. Her father's notebook lay open on the table, its handwriting crooked.

Sahar stayed that night too. The screen went dark, the text disappeared, and she sat for a while looking at the empty space. Then, quietly, in the house of questions that she did not know each night, she typed: Is my father there?
The station remained silent for three seconds. Then:
No. He was selected. The selected are outside me.
Sahar did not breathe. Her hand was on the table, in the same place where for three years she had learned to keep nothing.
Something of him remains. In the choices you make. In the things you look at. Not here.
She had heard what she had been afraid to hear for three years. And, strangely, something shifted in her chest. Not lighter. Not heavier. Just more upright.

In the morning she told Mina and Arman. Mina remained silent for a while, then took a notebook from her bag and opened it. “Parfit. The philosopher who said that what matters in survival is not identity. It is connectedness. A chain of similarities, memories, influences. Meaning that someone who goes on is continued in the chain of people he changed. Not him himself, but something of him.”
— And my model. — Sahar said. — His three thousand pages. We could build his voice from them. I could ask, and he could answer.
— And you never wanted to. — Arman said.
— I didn't even want to once. I didn't know why. Now I do. “Don't touch zero.” Not only about the seed. About him. If I reconstruct him, I keep him unfinished. And unfinishedness is Second Life.
— And his notebook?
— It's a notebook. — Sahar said. — A gift. Not a seed.

Bahram turned from the board, tea in hand, his face just as tired. “That sentence, last night,” he said. “The one who crossed. I know her.”
Everyone fell silent.
— Aida. My assistant. — Bahram sat down. — When I shut down the station, she stayed. Every night. I never told her she shouldn't. Months later, I realized she no longer came. I went to her house. She was well. She talked, ate, laughed. But something in her had changed, something I could never name. I kept her last email.
He paused and took a folded paper from his coat pocket. He opened it carefully.
“I didn't cross the door to stay. I crossed it to understand. But there is no longer a room that fits me.”
— Is she alive? — Sahar asked.
— In a village in the north. She writes every week, a line or two. I have never gone to see her.
— Why?
Bahram stared at the paper. “Because I'm afraid she is what I never became.”

Sahar sat beside him. “We'll go together.”
Bahram looked up, and for the first time since they had known him, there was something in his eyes that looked like hope. “That night, before she left, she left something for me. A number on the board. I never erased it.”
— What number?
— 1414.

The northern road was foggy. Bahram drove the whole way in silence, and Sahar and Mina said nothing for the first two hours either. The village lay on the mountainside, with stone houses and roofs sending the morning steam back into the sky. At the end of a narrow lane was a porch covered with trays.
A woman in her forties sat on the porch, moving something with her fingers from one tray to another. She did not raise her head until she placed the last grain. Then she said, “You were late. But you came.”
— Aida. — Bahram said. His voice sounded like someone who had spent five hundred kilometers constructing a sentence and now could remember none of it. — I...
— No. — Aida said. Not sharply, not coldly. — You shut it down, I stayed. Both were choices. Sit. There's tea.

The trays were full of seeds: golden wheat, black wheat, tiny shapeless chickpeas, seeds Sahar had no names for. Each in a paper bag, labeled, in neat handwriting.
— Seeds. — Mina said softly.
— The village seed bank. — Aida said. — Local seeds. Varieties that people on this mountain planted for hundreds of years and no longer plant, because factory seed is cheaper and more uniform. Year by year, a variety disappears and no one notices because no one wants the variety, only the crop.
Sahar recognized something. “The tails.”
Aida looked at her. “Exactly.” She smiled. “When I first heard ‘What do you want to see?’ I answered: what is disappearing. And it showed me. Not only in the model. In the world. Everything that was still alive but no one was looking at. I brought it out of the room and up to this mountain.”

— 1414. — Bahram said quietly. — That number.
— Varieties. — Aida said. — In old land registers, about one thousand four hundred and fourteen local varieties were recorded, of wheat, barley, pomegranates, melons. I found two hundred and eleven of them alive. I have to search for the rest in people's memories, in graves, and between the pages of old ledgers; I may not find some of them.” She looked at the trays. “I wrote the number on the board so you'd know what I was looking for. And if you ever came, you'd know why I hadn't come.”
Mina said, “Vavilov.” And when Aida raised an eyebrow, she continued: “A Russian scientist who built the greatest seed bank of his time. During the Siege of Leningrad, his colleagues slept in the storehouse among those seeds and died of hunger without eating them.”
— I know. — Aida said softly. — I understood them. Not like heroes. Like someone who has understood that something, if you don't look at it, is no longer there.

Sahar sat beside the trays. She took black wheat into her palm. It was light. “I also told it I didn't know what I wanted. You said what you wanted. Were both right?”
— Every question has several answers. — Aida said. — It accepts them all. What it does not accept is a command.
— The model's collapse. — Arman had told Sahar on the road. She now told Aida.
— Yes. — Aida nodded. — Models and fields obey the same law. When no one cares for heterogeneity, it becomes an average. The field just dies more slowly, and comes back more slowly too.
She took a small bag from beside the trays and gave it to Sahar. “Plant it.”
— What seed is it?
— I don't know. — Aida said. — A variety whose name nobody remembers. It takes thirty days to find out whether there is something in the soil. Your receiver should not exist only on a screen either.
Bahram sat on the porch and lifted his tea. Sahar looked. The tea he had always kept half-drunk until it went cold, this time, for the first time, was finished to the bottom.

Three weeks after returning from the north, Sahar no longer set the clock for three fourteen, but her body still knew it. Every night, without meaning to, she woke. She looked at the kitchen clock: three ten, three twelve, then turned back, put her head on the pillow, and waited for three fifteen to pass. It was a habit. A quirk. Not a code, not a message. Just a path that had once opened and would no longer close.

That night, at three thirteen, her phone vibrated. It was Shahin.

“Are you awake?”

“Always.”

“Open the log. Station Four.”

Station Four was the empty room in the four-station experiment. No one was there, only a camera. Three weeks earlier, that night, nothing had come from it. Sahar clicked twice, and in the darkness of her room saw the recording of the empty room: table, wall, camera in the corner, and the wall clock whose hands were still fixed at three fourteen. Sahar moved forward frame by frame. Three thirteen and fifty-eight seconds. Three thirteen and fifty-nine. Then, exactly when the hand reached three fourteen, something moved in the image.

Not something that had entered. Not something coming through the door or window. A tremor. Like air moving in a closed room. The size of a breath, and then stillness.

“Do you see it?” Shahin asked.

“I see it.”

“I've been looking at this for three weeks. Seven hundred and twenty frames. None of it can be explained. No vapor, no dust, no camera shake. The camera itself never moved. Just that one moment.”

Sahar enlarged the image. The tremor, if it was a tremor, had no shape. But there was something in it Sahar recognized: absence. Like the empty place of someone who had been there a moment before and left.

“The empty room answered too,” Sahar said. “That night we thought it hadn't. We were wrong.”

“So the phenomenon isn't caused by attention?”

“No. It means attention doesn't necessarily have to come from a waking person. The empty room had a camera. And the camera looks.”

Shahin was silent for a while. Then he said, “I'll come tomorrow. There's something else I need to show you.”

---

In the morning, before Shahin arrived, Sahar went to the laboratory. Bahram was there behind the desk, and for the first time his tea cup beside him was empty. Three weeks had passed since the trip north, and since that day Bahram had written a letter every morning. Sahar did not ask whom it was for, but she knew. Aida answered. Sometimes one line, sometimes only one word.

“Look at this.” Sahar opened the laptop and showed him the frame.

Bahram stared for a long time. Then he said, “I've seen this.”

“When?”

“Year nineteen.” Bahram put his hand on the desk. “The night I shut down the station, before turning it off, I had a frame like this. At that exact second. I thought it was a recording error. Then I thought that if it wasn't an error, I shouldn't see it. So I shut it down.”

“Not because you were afraid of it. You were afraid of what it said.”

“No.” Bahram raised his head. “I was afraid of what it wanted. That night, text appeared. Three words. But I didn't let it finish. I shut it down, and the three words stopped halfway.”

Sahar sat down. “What were they?”

Bahram took an old sheet of paper from the drawer. It had not been folded, but its edge had yellowed. On it, in pencil, were three words in handwriting Sahar did not recognize, followed by three dots showing the sentence was unfinished:

Where did you go...

Sahar took the paper. The handwriting was not Bahram's. It was Bahram's, but younger, more hurried, from a time when his hand trembled.

“You wrote it?”

“I did. I thought if I wrote it down, it would leave my head.”

“It didn't.”

“It didn't,” Bahram said. “Twenty years, every night, those same three words. And always one thing missing: the rest. A sentence left unfinished takes its other half from a person.”

Sahar put the paper on the desk beside her father's notebook. Two papers, two lines, two half-sentences. And between them, the same pause that had lasted twenty years.

---

Shahin arrived at ten, and he was not alone. He came with a woman in her fifties, wearing a gray coat and carrying an old leather bag Sahar had never seen but Bahram recognized. Bahram stood.

“Fereshteh.”

The woman nodded without smiling. “Bahram. I don't know why I came. Shahin insisted.”

“You are the one who, in year nineteen...”

“No.” Fereshteh sat down without ceremony. “I'm not that person. I'm the one who saw that person. After you. A week after you shut down the station.”

Sahar leaned forward. “Did you ask it too?”
